PRESSURE   SENSATION  —  PRESUMPTION 


Histories  of  Philosophy  by  UEBERWEG- 
HELNZE,  WINDELBAND,  ERDMANN  (the  former 
give  bibliographies).  For  recent  literature- 
see  the  '  Berichte '  in  the  Arch.  f.  syst.  Philo 
sophic.  (J.H.T.) 

Pressure  Sensation  [Lat.  2)ressura-  a 
burden]  :  Ger.  Druckempfindung ;  Fr.  sensa 
tion  de  pression ;  Ital.  sensazione  di  pres- 
sione  (or  bar  lea).  A  sensation  obtainable 
( i )  from  the  '  pressure  spots '  of  skin  and 
mucous  membrane,  (2)  from  striped  muscle, 
and  possibly  (3)  from  joints.  Cf.  ARTICULAE 
SENSATION. 

Pressure  and  pain  are  perhaps  the  oldest 
sense-processes  in  kind.  On  its  intensive 
side,  cutaneous  pressure  follows  Weber's  law. 
Both  the  cutaneous  pressure  and  the  articular 
sensation  are  endowed  with  the  attribute  of 
extent,  and  possess  local  signature. 

The  following  points  may  be  noticed: — (i) 
Pressure  stimuli  give  rise,  under  favourable 
conditions,  to  two  sensations,  the  primary 
and  the  secondary  pressure.  The  explanation 
has  been  sought  in  a  double  conduction  by 
the  spinal  cord,  and  in  the  existence  of  centri 
fugal  fibres  of  the  sensory  nerves.  (2)  There 
is  a  close  interrelation  of  the  senses  of  pres 
sure  and  temperature :  cold  and  hot  bodies 
are  heavier  than  bodies  of  equal  weight  at  a 
neutral  temperature.  (3)  Under  certain  con 
ditions — constancy  of  articularand  inconstancy 
of  cutaneous  stimulation — there  is  an  outward 
reference  of  sensation,  e.  g.  to  the  tip  of  the 
stick  held  in  the  hand.  Cf.  HAPTICS.

Pressure  Spot :  Ger.  Druckpunkt ;  Fr. 
point  de  pression ;  Ital.  punto  di  pressione 
(punti  barici).  A  spot  of  the  skin  evincing 
peculiar  sensitiveness  to  stimulations  of  pas 
sively  supported  weight.  See  PRESSURE 
SENSATION,  and  WEIGHT  SENSATION.  Cf.  the 
remarks  made  under  TEMPERATURE  SPOT  on 
the  use  of  the  word  '  spot '  (in  preference  to 
'  point'). 

Literature :  M.  BLIX,  Zeitsch.  f.  Bio!.,  xx
